title: Pet shop fish room: pumps, heaters, UV lamps, carbon and glass tanks
summary: A pet shop's fish room and reptile wall hold mains water pumps, air pumps and blowers, 50–500 W heaters, thermostats, UV-C sterilisers, sealed bags of activated carbon, filter media and a lot of glass tanks. Allow about an hour. The main dangers are wet mains wiring, mercury in broken UV lamps, glass, and foul tank water.

steps.text: Look from the door. If any animals are still alive, deal with them first or leave them to someone who can. Don't put a hand into a tank or vivarium you haven't seen into: large reptiles and snakes bite, and some shops hold species that are dangerous. Keep every lid on until you know what is inside.
Open doors and windows and air the room before you stay long. Wear gloves and a mask. Stagnant tanks smell. Reptile enclosures carry Salmonella, and fish tank water can infect cuts.
steps.warn: Wash your hands and arms with soap and clean water afterwards, and don't eat or touch your face while you work.

steps.text: Switch off the circuits for the racks at the breaker, then unplug the power strips from the wall. Check floor-level sockets and strips for damp, and prove the circuit dead with a meter (see safety_mains_isolation).
steps.warn: Fish rooms are wet and everything is plugged in at floor height. Never work on wet plugs, cords or strips with the power on.

steps.text: Siphon water out of the tanks you will move or open, down to the sump or below the lowest fitting. Carry the water out in buckets and pour it on soil, never into a well or a stream you drink from. Don't try to move a full tank: a 100 litre tank weighs well over 100 kg.
Take the heaters. Unplug them, then wait 15 minutes for them to cool before lifting them out. Wipe them dry and keep each with its cord and suction cups. Look for cracks in the glass tube.
steps.warn: A glass heater that is switched on out of water can crack or burst. Never plug one in until it is back in water.

steps.text: Take the UV-C sterilisers whole. Unplug them and lift out the sealed unit with its hoses. Don't open the housing, and don't plug the lamp in outside it. Pad each unit in a box.
steps.warn: The lamps contain mercury and the glass breaks easily. If one breaks, open the windows, leave for 15 minutes, don't vacuum, and pick up beads with card and tape (see the mercury hazard). Never look at a lit UV-C lamp.

steps.text: Take the pumps and blowers. Unplug each and pull its tubing off. Check that the shaft or impeller turns by hand. Air pumps and blowers from the central air system are often under the racks or in the back room. Wipe pumps clean; rinse the impellers in clean water.

Take the reptile gear: heat mats, ceramic heat emitters, bulb holders, thermostats and their probes. Unplug and let ceramic emitters cool. Keep each thermostat with its probe and cable. Don't cut into a heat mat or fold it hard: the wire inside breaks.
Take the LED lights and their plug-in adapters, with the lamp bars still attached to their cables. Note the label volts (12–24 V is common) and the polarity of the plug.

Take the glass tanks you can carry. Empty them, lay each on its side on a thick blanket or cardboard, and cut the silicone along each seam with a long knife or a taut wire, working from the corner. Carry panes upright on their edges, in pairs, one hand on each side.
steps.warn: Aquarium glass is thick and breaks into long, sharp shards. Wear thick gloves and eye protection and keep panes upright on edge.

steps.text: Take the filter media and fittings. Sealed bags of carbon, floss, ceramic rings and sponges are the best; used media from running tanks is dirty. Rinse used sponges in clean water and sun-dry them. Coil airline tubing and bag clamps, valves and fittings by type. Leave any gas cylinder (CO2 for plants) standing upright and capped.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Water pumps.** Submersible and inline mains pumps (10–200 W) move water for a rain tank, a solar water heater, a gravity filter or an irrigation line. Run them from an inverter and battery, or look for the 12/24 V ones.
- **Air pumps and blowers.** Linear air pumps and ring blowers (40–750 W) give steady air for aerating water, drying, or feeding a small forge or rocket stove. A big blower is worth carrying.
- **UV-C sterilisers.** A sealed lamp and ballast of 9–55 W. UV-C kills bacteria and viruses in clear water that flows past it slowly, so it can be a second step after a filter. It was made to control algae, not drinking-water treatment, so don't rely on it alone: boil or filter as well (see skill_solar_disinfection).
- **Activated carbon.** Unopened bags take out chlorine, bad taste and many chemicals as a filter stage. Rinse it until the water runs clear. It does not kill germs.
- **Filter sponges and floss.** A first, coarse stage for a gravity filter (see build_gravity_water_filter).
- **Heaters, heat mats and ceramic emitters.** Mains heating elements of 25–500 W. Good for warming a brooder, a seedling tray, a cold-frame or a fermenting bucket. Use them only through a working thermostat.
- **Thermostats and probes.** Mains on/off or pulse thermostats with a temperature probe: a ready-made temperature controller for a heater, a brooder or an incubator (they only switch heat on: they can't cool).
- **LED lights and drivers.** 12–24 V lamps and their adapters, good for a 12 V lighting system (see build_led_lighting_12v).
- **Glass tanks.** Glass panes for cold frames, a small solar oven window or a lantern. Tanks themselves make seed starters and storage for dry goods once clean.
- **Tubing, pipe, tubs and buckets.** Silicone airline tubing and tubs make water storage and irrigation parts.

## Variations

- Big chain stores have rack systems with a central sump, a UV unit and a large pump, so there is much more per tank to take.
- Saltwater (marine) systems have protein skimmers, salt and test kits: salt-water salts are useful but not food grade.
- Garden centres have pond pumps, pond liners and pond filters of the same kind.

## What to leave

- Live food, dead fish and anything dead or rotten.
- Gas cylinders unless you know what they hold.
- Medicines for pets unless you can read the label.
